results.title: long-term dependencies. Including this and our new perspective, we highlight two critical issues of high recency bias. The first is that a recommendation system with high recency bias seriously lacks serendipity, which is one of the major requirements a fine recommendation system ought to satisfy, as it repeatedly suggests items similar to only those the user recently interacted with. This monotony can quickly bore out user, and further lead to user disengagement. Second, high recency bias means the recommendation system fails to model the entire session into mining user preference, which was the primary goal of sequential recommendation system, and pigeonhole into only users most recent interests, as mentioned in [21]. Still, we lack an universal method to measure this recency bias in existing sequential recommendation models. [21] does measure recency bias, but this is only demonstrated in a reinforcement based setting, not universally applicable to many existing sequential recommendation models, also resulting in the absence of measurement experimental results of recency bias of existing models.

results.title: [2508.03606] Demystifying Sequential Recommendations: Counterfactual Explanations via Genetic Algorithms

item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating recency, repetition, and incidental sequence associations. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) proposes quantifying excessive reliance on recent interactions. [BSARec (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28747) identifies self-attention oversmoothing, suggesting that weak order sensitivity can reflect collapsed sequence representations. [Counterfactual Explanations via Genetic Algorithms (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) searches for minimal history edits that change recommendations; [CoDeR (2025)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/33379) and [CoDeR+ (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3778863) address demand shifts versus noisy signals. Earlier, directly relevant [Repetition and Exploration (2023)](https://staff.fnwi.uva.nl/m.derijke/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/li-2023-repetition.pdf) finds repetition shortcuts and shared-embedding bias, including inappropriate repeat recommendations for exploration users.\n\nSuggested diagnostic synthesis: construct training-prefix next-item holdouts; compare untouched histories, recent versus distant edits, order-only permutations, and equal-count replacements matched on training popularity and title/description similarity. Separate repeated item IDs from recurring semantic interests. Keep candidates, sequence length, padding, and inference randomness fixed; use unchanged-history reruns to establish numerical stability. Measure paired target-rank changes, score margins, top-10 overlap, and representation shifts, stratified by history length, repetition, and target novelty. Combine perturbations with encoder ablations or hidden-state similarity checks to investigate positional dependence and oversmoothing; attention weights alone cannot establish the mechanism. These are proposed controls synthesized from the literature, not a published unified protocol. Ranking sensitivity demonstrates dependence of the fitted model on edited inputs; it does not establish causal effects on real user preferences, especially when replacements create implausible histories."}
